body:
## Module 1 in two minutes

**You can already use the tools. This series is about what to decide.** No fundamentals, no prompting primer, no tool tour, no vendor showcase — the exclusions are the product.

**The credibility chain: personal fluency → functional transformation → enterprise standing.** You cannot redesign your function's work without knowing what the tools do, and you cannot hold a position in a C-suite argument without having transformed your function. The chain rests on a mechanism rather than a statistic: **judgment about where this technology is reliable is not transferable from a briefing.**

**Executive-altitude practice aims the model at your reasoning, not your output.** Rehearsal before a decision you own — committing your position first, then demanding the strongest case against it. Pattern-finding across your own record. Interrogating it on something you know cold, which is the fastest route to calibrated skepticism because **you will catch it being confidently wrong in your own domain.**

**Delegated fluency produces confident wrongness at the top of the house** — where you lose the ability to interrogate what you are told, and where nobody above you is positioned to correct the belief before it reaches procurement and policy.

## The standard

**Never "how confident are you?" Always "what did you actually do last quarter?"**

Self-reported confidence about AI tracks marketing exposure, temperament and recency — not capability — and it is inflated at senior levels, where admitting uncertainty currently reads as being behind. Behaviour is checkable. And where you cannot check, **the inability to check is the finding.**

## What the full module adds

Why the supporting survey is stated and then set aside — 264 self-selected respondents, a publisher with an interest, and a correlation with no direction — and why leading on it would have discredited everything after. The two mechanisms of the delegation trap. **The CFO objection**, taken seriously: second-hand judgment works where an audit apparatus exists, and here it does not yet, which makes the argument time-limited rather than eternal. Four executive practices to judge, only one of which builds judgment. And the activity: one practice, a real trigger, two runs, and one concrete thing it surfaced — where **a practice that fails contact with your calendar, reported precisely, beats enthusiasm.**
